contributions.headingText: Prostatic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a rare type of prostate cancer with squamous histology, defined by keratinization, keratin pearls, and intercellular bridges.
2C82.Y & XH0945 Other specified malignant neoplasms of prostate & Squamous cell carcinoma, NOS

SCC of the prostate gland most often arises in elderly patients with a history of hormone or radiation therapy, typically for prostatic adenocarcinoma {22212078; 15105655; 12588611}. Patients typically present with urinary obstruction, dysuria, haematuria, or bone pain from metastatic disease {22212078; 15105655; 14730162}. Pelvic lymph node metastases and osteolytic bone metastases are common. Serum PSA levels are usually not elevated. Radical prostatectomy or cystoprostatectomy is performed for organ-confined or locally advanced disease. There is no standard approach to metastatic disease; the use of chemotherapy and radiation therapy has been described in the literature, with questionable efficacy being reported {17407588; 14730162}.

The prognosis is poor, with a short survival time after diagnosis and no definitive treatment {22212078; 15105655}. SCC of the prostate is extremely rare {22212078; 15105655; 12588611; 11385309}. Most cases in the literature have been in patients who were > 70 years old.
In most reported cases, there is an association with previous hormone or radiation therapy for prostatic adenocarcinoma {15105655; 11385309}.

Studies in the literature and the sequence of disease progression suggest that treatment of adenocarcinoma precedes the development of SCC of the prostate {2459960; 14730162; 21627811; 30805072}. Lager et al. suggested that SCC of the prostate may arise because of adverse stimuli affecting the columnar cells, resulting in a loss of secretion of PSA and/or PAP with a concomitant gain in expression of keratin {2459960}. It has been speculated that SCC can arise from the pluripotent stem cells of the prostate gland or from squamous metaplasia of acini and prostatic ducts {12588611; 21627811}. Another hypothesis is that it might be a cellular transdifferentiation of acinar prostatic adenocarcinoma after cancer therapy such as androgen-deprivation therapy or radiation {21627811; 10754146; 7855985; 31882336}.

There are limited molecular data available because of the rarity of these tumours. However, several recent case reports, which applied next-generation sequencing–based technologies to 4 cases of locally recurrent and metastatic prostatic SCC, demonstrated TMPRSS2::ERG fusion in 3 of the tumours {29629426; 31882336; 32628337}. The remaining case harboured an SPOP mutation, which can also lead to ERG activation at the posttranslational level {31882336}. In contrast to the morphological features of SCC, which are nonspecific with respect to the site of origin, the presence of a TMPRSS2::ERG fusion essentially confirms the prostatic origin of the carcinoma. Also typical of acinar prostatic adenocarcinoma was the loss of PTEN in 3 cases, and a PTEN mutation was identified in the remaining case {29629426; 31882336; 32628337}.

Grossly, these tumours are yellow-white, firm, and often extensive, replacing most of the normal prostatic tissue. Compression of the prostatic urethra and invasion into the urinary bladder and other adjacent organs has been reported {22212078}.

The microscopic findings are similar to those observed in SCCs at other sites. Features include squamous architecture with keratinization and/or intercellular bridges and cellular anaplasia. There should be no glandular elements. Prostatic adenocarcinoma with squamous differentiation, local extension of bladder carcinoma with squamous differentiation, and metastatic SCC should be excluded {2602930; 458967; 21826130; 12497163; 21428844}. Gleason grading / grade groups are not applicable; these tumours can be graded as well differentiated, moderately differentiated, or poorly differentiated, based on the degree of keratinization and cellular atypia. Tumours lack expression of PSA, PAP, and PSMA, and the show positivity for p63, 34βE12, CK5/6, and CK14 {17407588; 15105655}. AMACR can be positive {21627811}.

Essential: squamous architecture with keratinization and/or intercellular bridges; cellular anaplasia; absence of glandular differentiation; exclusion of prostatic adenocarcinoma with squamous differentiation, local invasion by bladder carcinoma with squamous features, and metastatic SCC.
The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) and Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) classification applies to prostatic SCC {29325693}.

SCC of the prostate is an aggressive disease with a poor prognosis. These tumours are often detected at the time of transurethral resection subsequent to urinary obstruction and patients have advanced disease at presentation {21627811; 14730162; 17407588}. The average survival period is usually short, ranging from 6 to 24 months in the literature, with no known prognostic factors {15105655; 22212078; 14730162}.
